newsitem.title: UK: POLL-UK rates seen rising to 6.75 pct next week.
newsitem.headline: POLL-UK rates seen rising to 6.75 pct next week.

text.p: British interest rates are expected to rise next week because the budget announced on Wednesday did not do enough to quell consumer spending, a Reuters survey showed on Thursday.
Twenty-one out of 24 contributors to the survey expect the Bank of England's monetary policy committee to announce an increase in interest rates after a meeting on July 10.
Of these, 17 saw official rates rising to 6.75 percent from their current 6.5 percent level and four forecast a 0.5 percentage point rise to seven percent.
Two respondents said rates would not rise until August's monetary council meeting, when rates would rise to 6.75 percent.
One contributor said he was unsure if interest rates would change this time, but that if there were a move, it would be to 6.75 percent.
"The budget was not tight enough to hold back consumers. Brown's budget was disappointing and will not contain the overheating economy," said Mark Wall, UK economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.

Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown, in the first budget of the new Labour government, forecast consumer expenditure would grow by 4.5 percent in 1997 and four percent in 1998 from 3.5 percent in 1996.
Those who predicted a 50 basis-point rise said Britain was still in the early stages of a consumer boom which would not peak until 1998.

"The momentum of consumer demand will ensure strong above-trend growth this year and next. We are already operating at full capacity and inflation will become a problem," said Stewart Robertson, UK economist at Lombard Street Research.
Brown forecast gross domestic product (GDP) growth at 3.25 percent this year, well above estimated trend growth of 2.25 to 2.5 percent, from 2.5 percent in 1996.
Several analysts disagreed with the Chancellor's forecast of 2.5 percent GDP growth in 1998 and seven said they saw interest rates climbing slowly and peaking next year.

"We see interest rates peaking next year because sterling strength will continue to feed into subdued inflation data for at least a year," said Stewart Newnham, international economist at First Chicago.
"But it does create a policy conundrum for the Bank of England (BoE)."

Sterling reached a five-year high of 2.9430 marks on July 2. The dilemma for the BoE and the monetary council is that further interest rate rises will worsen problems for an already sluggish manufacturing sector.
Most of the contributors, 14 out of 21, expected interest rates to peak by the end of this year.
Six out of 22 said they saw base rates peaking at 7.25 percent and six expected the top to be 7.50 percent. Four expected the high at eight percent and three at seven percent.

"The case for interest rates over seven percent has been weakened with the tightening envisaged in the budget. It goes quite a way to restoring the balance between fiscal and monetary policy," said Keith Edmonds, chief analyst at IBJ International.
Brown announced a net fiscal tightening of 5.5 billion sterling this year and 4.75 billion in 1998.
One contributor said he expected base rates to peak above eight percent and one predicted a high at nine percent.
Mark Hale, general manager of research at Sakura Finance, who does not expect a rise next week, is the only contributor forecasting a peak at 6.75 percent, which he sees happening in August.
"We've already had two hikes which have not been fully felt. Higher mortgage rates are just coming through," said Hale.

"There is also a lot of optimism that interest rates in Germany will not rise until next year. Higher UK interest rates and higher sterling may have further unfortunate consequences on manufacturing."
Andy Cates, UK economist at UBS, also believes there will be no rate rise next week.
"They will not want to say to the financial markets that they did not view the budget favourably," he said.
